vignette:
He sits in the cockpit of the Boeing 777, the pre-flight checklist nearly complete. The faint hum of the auxiliary power unit vibrates through his seat, a sound he has heard tens of thousands of times. As the first officer calls out the final items, a sudden high-pitched whine from the air conditioning pack cuts through the cabin. His hands freeze on the throttles. For a split second, he is not in a modern airliner at 35,000 feet. He is nineteen years old, crouched in a muddy rice paddy near Da Nang, the scream of an incoming mortar round filling his ears. His heart hammers, sweat beads on his forehead, and he has to fight the urge to duck beneath the instrument panel. The first officer looks at him with concern. “Captain? You okay?” He forces a nod, pulling his mind back to the present, but the tremor in his hands lingers for the next hour.

That was 1970. He was a young conscript from a small island nation in the South Pacific, shipped halfway around the world to fight in a war that made little sense to him. His unit patrolled villages along the central highlands, searching for Viet Cong. On a hot November afternoon, his squad walked into an ambush. The first burst of automatic fire tore through the man walking beside him, a friend named Leo from the next village. The spray of blood and the sharp, metallic smell of it—mixed with damp earth and burning gunpowder—are details he has never been able to forget. He spent the next eight hours pinned down, firing blindly into the treeline, watching Leo’s body grow cold in the mud. When the medevac finally arrived, they lifted him out of the mud, his hands shaking so badly he could not hold his rifle.

He returned home in 1971, quiet and thin. He married his high school sweetheart, found work as a bush pilot flying cargo between islands, and slowly built a life. The nightmares started early but he never spoke of them. He learned to push the memories away by staying busy. By his forties, he was flying commercial jets—long hauls across the Pacific. The discipline of the cockpit gave him structure. Checklists, procedures, the constant demands of instrument scanning: these kept his mind occupied. He could fly for fourteen hours and not think of the war once. But the triggers always found him. The smell of jet fuel sometimes brought him back to the smell of a burning village. A sudden loud bang in the cabin, like an oxygen generator deploying, made him flinch so hard he once spilled coffee on his uniform.

Now at sixty-three, he is still flying, but the cracks are widening. His sleep is nearly gone. He wakes three or four times a night, drenched in sweat, Leo’s face staring at him from the fog of a dream. He avoids any movie or news report about war. His wife has learned not to touch him from behind—he will whirl around with fists clenched. On his days off, he stays in the garage, rebuilding an old outboard motor, hoping the mechanical work will quiet the static inside his head. It does not. At the dinner table, his wife tries to talk about their grandson’s school play, but he hears only a buzzing, then the distant echo of machine-gun fire.

Last week, during a flight from Sydney to Los Angeles, a passenger had a seizure in the aisle. The flight attendant’s urgent call over the intercom hit his ears like a radio crackling with a fire-mission order. He froze for what felt like minutes, the First Officer having to repeat his name three times before he snapped to. He handed over the controls without a word. The rest of the flight he sat rigid, staring at the horizon, unable to speak. His PCL-5 score from the company-authorized psychological assessment was seventy-five—far above the threshold for PTSD. He does not call it that. He just calls it “the price of having been there.” And tonight, as he taxis the 777 to the gate, he will walk past the cockpit door, down the jet bridge, and into the parking lot, his shoulders squared, his face blank, carrying a war that ended fifty years ago.
